title: Why the Team That Builds a Power Plant Isn't the Same Team That Runs It
excerpt: Across the US, new power generation projects continue moving through development and construction.
html:
Across the US, new power generation projects continue moving through development and construction.

This year alone, developers plan to add 6.3 GW of new natural-gas-fired generating capacity, with combined-cycle plants accounting for more than half of that total.

New U.S. electric generating capacity expected to reach a record high in 2026 - U.S. Energy Information Administration (EIA)

While more projects come to fruition, it becomes clear that building capacity is only part of the equation. Each stage, from construction through commissioning, demands specialized teams before the plant transitions to full operations.

The teams responsible for building and testing a plant are rarely the same professionals who will ultimately operate it.

Building the Plant

(The Power Plant Workforce Lifecycle)

As with every project, once planning is complete, construction begins.

A successful build relies on a diverse team, including project, construction, and site managers who oversee progress and maintain standards.

Work is done to make sure that the necessary structures, pipes, electrical systems, and controls are in place. As power plants are highly complex facilities, specialist contractors are needed to install critical equipment and systems.

As diverse as the teams are, the work is just as varied. Contractors and engineering teams work on separate parts of the project, often coordinated by project staff along with the schedule, suppliers, and technical issues.

Each stage is important, but construction establishes the foundation for all subsequent phases.

They are working to complete the project. However, the goal is to ensure the plant is fully prepared for commissioning.

The Transition Through Commissioning

Commissioning is, simply put, the testing stage between construction and full operation. It doesn’t mean the construction team is cast aside.

In fact, it’s the opposite. Their expertise is vital during this period.

While the building may be finished on the surface, it would be irresponsible to go straight to operating.

This is the natural workforce transition point. Construction workers may still be fixing and finishing things, while the future operations staff begin their involvement, working together to identify and resolve any outstanding issues.

This isn’t just a case of homing in on one section, but the whole project.

Equipment and systems need to be checked, making sure their installation has been carried out correctly and that different systems can work together as intended. This culminates in transferring knowledge across the teams and preparing and training personnel for later operations.

The purpose of this stage is to prove the finished plant can become an operating plant.

Moving Into Operations

Once operations begin, priorities change.

With the project phase concluded, attention turns to maintaining safe and reliable plant operations for the long term.

The workforce shifts accordingly, with operators, engineers, supervisors, and management taking on permanent roles. Duties merge into monitoring and controlling plant processes, overseeing equipment performance, conducting maintenance, addressing faults, and managing shifts to ensure safe and reliable operation.

The workforce is therefore more permanent and repetitive in purpose, focused on keeping the plant operating for the rest of its life.

Beyond the Build

The diversity of needs for power plant projects is high due to the requirements of every stage, but it is still highly purposeful.

Completion and operation result from fulfilling each preceding requirement in turn, from building and commissioning to the stage where operations can run safely and reliably over the long term.

A smooth transition is not always guaranteed. To mitigate the risk of disrupting the process, the right people at the right time become a necessity, with knowledge carried forward from one team to the next.

Long-term success depends on how effectively the workforce transitions from construction into operation.

title: Why Planned Power Plant Outages Create a Different Hiring Challenge.
excerpt: Challenge. The importance of power plants is difficult to overstate.
html:
Challenge. The importance of power plants is difficult to overstate.

They can be responsible for homes, factories, towns, cities, and even entire transportation systems. When something has this much influence on daily life, it becomes crucial to maintain.

They’re built to operate continuously, but keeping them running also requires knowing when to stop.

The machinery used requires maintenance, inspections, repairs, and upgrades. Obviously, this isn’t something you can do as and when. There’s no predicting when a generator could go out, and there’s no instant knowledge of what’s gone wrong. Leaving this to chance isn't viable, as the outcome isn't guaranteed. It can be difficult or even impossible to do what’s needed while equipment is still in service.

Power plants understand this, and they’re already ahead of the curve. Planned outages are a controlled window used to carry out these services. Despite this only being done over a limited period, it can completely change a plant's workforce needs.

The question then becomes: how do operators ensure they have the right people in place to meet these demands?

What Makes Outage Staffing Difficult

In a typical operation, power plants have an established workforce to keep the site running. This changes with a planned outage. There are more duties and more volume to manage. The original team may not be able to manage this alone, so consequently, the need for specialists and contractors arises.

However, the challenge is not just simply finding more people. It’s finding the right people.

Different stages of the outage require different expertise. Some workers may only be needed for particular parts of the schedule. Someone carrying out an inspection, for example, may be needed before another team can begin repairs or replacements. It’s all variable, depending on the work needed.

With this becoming standard practice, plants have gained insight into the work that needs to be carried out and the processes required. This has allowed them to understand the length of time needed for an outage window.

This window is very important for them to work within. The period is accounted for, meaning any work taking longer than expected can delay what follows and create stress on the planned return to service.

This, combined with the possibility that inspections uncover problems not previously fully understood, culminates in a situation that plants need to be prepared for due to the additional work and potentially additional workforce required.

Preparing The Workforce Before The Outage

Recognizing the challenge is only the start. What matters is how you prepare.

For workforce planning to be effective, it starts with a clear outage scope.

Operators must first define the work needed to be completed, then identify the expertise needed at each stage and begin organizing internal teams, contractors, and specialist support.

Not every piece of work has to wait for the outage to begin either.

Preparation can be completed beforehand, and doing so can reduce the amount of work that’s competing for time and resources once equipment is taken out of service.

External specialists can also be integrated into the plan before they arrive on site. Understanding what they are responsible for, when their work can begin and how long it should take allows their involvement to fit around the wider outage rather than operate separately from it.

Flexibility remains essential.

Inspections may uncover additional requirements, so operators need contingency plans that allow for adjustments without overhauling the entire workforce strategy.

More Than Just Headcount

The workforce challenge begins well before the outage window, even if the outage itself is brief.

Operators need to understand the work required, identify the right expertise, and make sure those people are available at the right stages of the outage. With deadlines to meet and the possibility of unexpected work emerging, preparation becomes just as important as the work itself.

Successful outage staffing is not just about numbers. It is about having the right people, in the right place, at the right time.

title: What Happens If a Power Project Misses COD
excerpt: Getting a power project from blueprint to reality is rarely straightforward.
html:
Getting a power project from blueprint to reality is rarely straightforward.

It is not uncommon for years to pass between project milestones, with each stage presenting its own challenges before the plant ever reaches operation.

By the time construction commences, countless pieces start moving at once. Equipment needs to arrive, installations need to be completed, systems need to be tested, and eventually the plant needs to be commissioned.

All of this activity is coordinated with the expectation of meeting the Commercial Operation Date, or COD.

This is the point when the facility is expected to begin operations and commercial agreements can take effect.

Expectation, however, does not always become reality.

How a Project Works Towards COD

Once COD is set, the project has to be organized around reaching it.

This means working backwards from the final date and understanding what must be completed before each stage can begin.

The plant needs to be commissioned before COD, but before it can be commissioned, it needs to be tested. Before it can be tested, construction and installation need to be far enough along. To reach that point, the required equipment must be delivered to the site.

The process depends on what comes before it. Like making a cake, you can’t add the frosting before baking.

What can cause a missed COD?

This is why one slip in the process puts pressure on everything that follows.

Equipment might arrive later than expected, pushing installation back. Construction issues can take longer to resolve, while defects found late may require additional work before testing can continue.

Eventually, the time between the current stage and COD gets thinner.

Commissioning can create delays of its own. Failed tests may mean equipment needs to be adjusted, repaired, or replaced before it can be tested again.

Sometimes, problems sit outside the plant's control. Factors like grid connection, permitting delays or issues with contractors and suppliers can affect whether the project stays on schedule.

COD can be missed for a wide variety of reasons such as:

• Construction delays

• Equipment delivery delays • Commissioning failures or retesting

• Defects found late

• Grid/interconnection issues • Permitting or approval delays

• Contractor or supplier issues

While none are guaranteed, they’re all possible. The important thing to plan around is that any one of them can start eating into the time left before COD.

What happens when COD is missed?

While every effort has been made to avoid reaching this point, it remains a possibility.

At this point, the problem stops being purely about the schedule. The commercial operation has been pushed back. Now the focus turns to the delayed revenue, with the financial impact growing the longer the project remains behind schedule.

The cost doesn’t stop either. Project teams, contractors, and other requirements may still be needed for the remaining work. Handover can become delayed. Commercial commitments may need to be adjusted.

Potentially, one of the biggest consequences could be regarding the agreements and contracts in place.

An example of this came from a power purchase agreement involving the City of Garland, Texas and Delilah Solar Energy. Commercial operation had originally been expected by June 2022, but after the project passed 180 days beyond its Guaranteed Commercial Operation Date, the agreement resulted in Garland receiving a $2.5 million Early Termination Payment.

Some contracts can eventually give another party the right to terminate if the project fails to achieve commercial operation within the agreed limits.

This is what makes COD more than just a date.

A project can be delayed by weeks, but the consequences can last much longer.

title: What Happens After a Gas Turbine Upgrade?
excerpt: Gas turbines are one of the most crucial parts of gas-fired power plants, generating electricity by burning fuel, creating a hot, high-pressure gas, and spinning the turbine connected to the generator. In the context of a combined-cycle plant, this is
html:
Gas turbines are one of the most crucial parts of gas-fired power plants, generating electricity by burning fuel, creating a hot, high-pressure gas, and spinning the turbine connected to the generator. In the context of a combined-cycle plant, this is effectively the first stage of power generation.

With this being the case, the plant’s output effectively begins here, so upgrades here can have a significant effect on the overall performance, potentially increasing power output, improving efficiency, reliability, flexibility, or even just extending the life of equipment.

Now, on the surface, this seems like an upgrade on a sole piece of equipment. However, gas turbines don’t work alone. In fact, the system itself is much smarter than it may appear.

To minimize waste, the plant capitalizes on opportunities to create power through its current situation.

One of the most effective is the HRSG.

This piece of machinery captures hot exhaust gas, using that wasted heat to boil water and produce steam, before sending that steam into a steam turbine, which results in extra electricity.

What Changes After the Upgrade?

So what does any of this have to do with the turbine upgrade?

While the HRSG hasn’t changed, what’s being sent into it has.

An upgrade can change the exhaust leaving the gas turbine, including its temperature, how much is produced and how those conditions vary during operation. This can then affect how much steam the HRSG produces and how hard different parts of it are being worked.

This matters because the existing HRSG was designed to operate within an expected range of conditions from the turbine. Changing what enters the HRSG can mean the equipment is being asked to operate differently from before.

Understanding the Impact

To understand the implications of upgrading, engineers need to see the full picture.

This starts by looking at how the system operated before the upgrade and how it is expected to perform after. Comparing these conditions gives engineers a basis for checking whether the existing setup is still suitable and whether anything needs to change.

The outcome depends on the situation. In some scenarios, nothing may need to be amended. However, it’s not something to treat naively, as in others, the way the plant operates may need adjusting.

The aim is to understand whether the HRSG can properly support what the upgraded turbine is now capable of delivering.

Looking Beyond the HRSG

If the upgraded turbine delivers more energy to the HRSG, more steam will be produced. This introduces additional considerations beyond simply confirming the HRSG can handle the change.

The HRSG relies on control equipment that may also need to be evaluated for compatibility with new operating conditions. Turbine upgrades can require adjustments to feedwater control valves, temperature-control systems, and safety valves, depending on the assessment.

A recent example can be seen at West Phoenix CC5 in Arizona. A thermal performance project initially targeted an additional 55 MW from two combustion turbines, but the work extended beyond the turbines themselves. Changes were also made across the HRSGs and other plant equipment, with the completed project ultimately reporting a 58 MW increase.

Combined Cycle Journal - HRSG Forum 2024: General session covers all the bases⁠

Even when the HRSG can utilize the additional energy, downstream effects must be considered. The steam turbine must have sufficient capacity to process the increased steam flow. Otherwise, some of the benefits of the turbine upgrade may

not be realized.

Maximizing the benefits of a turbine upgrade may require modifications beyond the gas turbine, extending to other parts of the plant.

A Better Turbine, a Better Plant

A turbine upgrade only matters if the rest of the plant can use what it delivers. The real test isn’t the upgrade itself, but whether the whole system gets better as a result.

That’s why the engineering goes beyond the upgrade. Ultimately, the aim isn’t just a better turbine. It’s a better plant.

title: What Changes When Utilities Have to Buy Electrical Equipment Five Years Ahead?
excerpt: The United States, unsurprisingly, depends heavily on its electrical infrastructure, and it is a country driven by growth and innovation. This need only amplifies.
html:
The United States, unsurprisingly, depends heavily on its electrical infrastructure, and it is a country driven by growth and innovation. This need only amplifies.

Consequently, investment in electrical infrastructure has mirrored that, with new generation being built, existing grids being upgraded, and manufacturing expanding.

The issue, however, is that the transformers, switchgear, and breakers needed face limited manufacturing capacity. Large transformers can have lead times of around 3-4 years, while other critical electrical equipment can also take multiple years to arrive, pushing some utilities to plan around 5 years ahead.

So what happens when procurement has to move years earlier than the rest of the project?

The challenge is no longer just securing the equipment, but making technical and commercial decisions years before the wider project is fully settled.

Why procurement is moving earlier

For projects, the sequence is simple. When something is needed, engineers design and specify it, procurement buys the equipment, it arrives, and then it’s installed.

However, with substantial wait times, procurement can’t afford to wait until the design is completely finished.

Reuters reported in July that utilities and developers are ordering years ahead, making longer-term agreements with suppliers and looking overseas or at refurbished equipment. And this issue isn’t exaggerated. California's Roseville Electric has expanded its planning horizon to five years because of the problem.

Limited manufacturing capacity has created a long queue for production slots. Securing a slot, therefore, means getting your equipment into the future manufacturing schedule.

Some businesses have an advantage in this process, particularly larger customers because of their purchasing power and larger order volumes. This means not all buyers can solve the shortage equally well.

What changes when you buy before the project is settled

Transformers are difficult to build. Normally, you would spend time planning where it will go, how much capacity you need, and the exact design and spec before purchasing it.

That creates a tension: should you wait to preserve flexibility, or buy early?

Waiting means you risk it turning up years after you need it.

Buying early means you commit money and decisions while the project is still developing.

What changes while equipment is being built

While you must commit, early commitment carries risk.

From the decision to installation, so much can change. You have to account for factors such as:

• Expected electrical demand changing

• The factory not being built

• Project size increasing • Permitting taking longer • Network design changes

• Another substation becoming a priority

Even if none of this happens, engineering could still conclude a different specification would’ve been better.

You're effectively specifying equipment for the system you expect to have several years from now.

Equipment is expensive and slow to replace. So getting the prediction wrong isn’t a cheap mistake.

Can standardization give utilities more flexibility?

One reason manufacturing difficulty rises is that utilities use loads of different specifications.

Not every transformer is used for the same thing, which means they’re not a uniform design that can be rinsed and repeated. DOE has reported more than 80,000 distribution transformer specification variants across the US.

To address this, the industry is looking at making designs and components more interchangeable, potentially making them easier to manufacture and use across more locations.

The trade-off is between standardization and designing exactly what an individual project requires.

What does this change for engineering and procurement?

Engineers need to define project needs before procurement can secure equipment. With multi-year lead times, these discussions now start much earlier.

Procurement cannot focus only on price and delivery. They should also consider how fixed the specification is, what can change, whether another supplier could work, and whether securing a production slot is worth committing to before everything else is settled.

Designing the perfect specification means little if nobody can manufacture it until years after the project needs it.

Engineers may have to consider availability, alternative suppliers, and where a more standardized option could still meet the requirement. This puts more value on people who can understand both sides of the decision.

Procurement doesn’t need to become engineering, and engineers don’t need to become buyers, but neither side can operate completely separately when decisions are being made this far ahead.

When utilities are effectively buying equipment for the system they expect to have several years from now, getting the technical decision right is only part of the challenge. They also need to know whether they can realistically deliver on that decision, even as the project, market, and supply chain may have changed.

title: Can Power Generation Experience Transfer Into Nuclear
excerpt: Nuclear projects are highly complex. As are the roles.
html:
Nuclear projects are highly complex. As are the roles.

Many nuclear roles require professionals with nuclear knowledge and experience. That's the issue.

There are only so many experienced professionals, which makes the market highly competitive.

So how do employers look beyond the existing nuclear talent pool without compromising?

What Does Nuclear Actually Require?

Employers aren’t asking for nuclear experience for no reason.

Work in this sector is governed by strict procedures that define how tasks are performed, documented, and verified.

Safety is a priority, so these procedures are necessary and can't be improvised. As a result, training requirements vary by role. For example, Reactor Operators and Senior Reactor Operators must complete plant-specific training, simulator assessments, and written exams before the NRC can license them.

Some roles require even more rigorous checks. Where unescorted access is involved, candidates may undergo background investigations, drug and alcohol testing, and psychological evaluations.

Someone already working in the sector may understand not just the engineering, but the environment and expectations around it.

But those requirements are not identical for every role.

Where Can Experience From Other Sectors Fit?

Roles With Industry Overlap Some roles aren’t dependent on sector experience, allowing employers to look beyond people who have spent their entire careers in nuclear.

A maintenance engineer coming from gas generation may have spent years maintaining complex mechanical equipment in another environment. Their skill set may transfer, even without nuclear experience.

This can also apply to those within mechanical engineering, commissioning, construction, outages and project delivery.

The overlap is already being recognised at an industry level. The U.S. Department of Energy found significant overlap between jobs at coal and nuclear plants, with some workers able to transition with additional training or reskilling.

When looking outside of the sector, the question becomes: how much of the role is genuinely nuclear-specific, and how much is work that already exists elsewhere in power generation or heavy industry?

Skills That Carry Across

This becomes clear when you focus on the responsibilities and day-to-day tasks involved, rather than industry labels.

Engineers may bring years of experience troubleshooting pumps, valves, or rotating equipment. Professionals involved in outages may already be familiar with shutdown planning, contractor coordination, and working to strict procedures.

Those skills do not suddenly become irrelevant because of where they were developed.

But transferable does not mean interchangeable.

The question is whether the nuclear-specific parts of a role can be learned after someone joins, or whether they need to be present from day one. Where a position depends on specific licensing, qualifications or nuclear experience, experience from another sector cannot simply replace it.

Building the Nuclear Workforce

If someone can enter nuclear in a role where their existing experience is relevant, they can begin developing what they

previously lacked: nuclear experience.

As their experience grows, so can the roles available to them, although some positions will still require additional training or qualifications.

This grows the number of people with genuine nuclear experience, rather than leaving employers to continually compete for the same existing talent.

Every experienced nuclear professional gained that expertise somewhere. The real question for employers is not whether nuclear experience is important, but where it is truly essential.
